Q: How to handle and convert images with extension .nii.gz? A:

In addition to @fepegar answer - you probably don't want to save the images as .jpg format, since .jpg is a lossy-compression type, which means it losses important information. You should save the images to a lossless compression file types, such as .pgm for a single channel image, .png for 3 channels image, or .tiff (using python's package tifffile) for any other number of channels - which is probably what you'd want in this case.

pip install tifffile

import tifffile as tiff
tiff.imwrite(file_path, image, dtype=np.float32)  # Save the image as a TIFF file as FP32

Q: ImagePullBackOff error because of DNS resolve problem A:

The nslookup command shows that DNS Server is "10.41.128.98". but why pod log says like "lookup my.docker.proxy.com on [2001:100:100:11::a]:53: server misbehaving;"? It seems like DNS server is "[2001:100:100:11::a]".

A system can have multiple DNS servers configured – and it's very common to have the same DNS server via both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

When you have multiple DNS server addresses, usually programs will try them in some specific order. The error message looks like it came from a Golang program, and I don't know what Golang does exactly, but I believe it queries all the OS-configured servers until gets an answer – much like the DNS functions in the OS itself.

Nslookup differs in this regard, and always uses only the first server that was configured. So for example, if your OS has both 10.41.128.98 and 2001:100:100:11::a configured, then the OS will use both servers, but nslookup will always use the first one unless told otherwise.

And secondly, Why nslookup command shows "** server can't find my.docker.proxy.com: REFUSED", even though it already show 'my.docker.proxy.com' address is 10.251.186.33?

That's because nslookup actually makes two DNS queries – one for A records, one for AAAA records (IPv4 and IPv6 addresses respectively) – and the incompetently written DNS server at 10.41.128.98 returns an error code for the 2nd query instead of just returning an empty response.

(Maybe it's an internal proxy that is trying to block IPv6?)

A nameserver's authority is for the whole name, and cannot be specific to just individual record types – either the nameserver handles queries for the name for all types, or doesn't recognize it at all. The error code "REFUSED" should only be used when the nameserver doesn't handle that name at all. (And generally a resolver – the client-facing DNS server – should never return this error to its clients at all, since it handles requests for "all" names.)

Since the first query (for A records) succeeded, that means the nameserver is recognizing the name (as expected from a resolver, whose job is to handle all names), and therefore queries for all other types must also succeed. Even if the nameserver doesn't have the requested types, but the name exists overall, the correct response would be a success reply with 0 records of that type. By returning a REFUSED, the nameserver is contradicting itself by saying that it recognizes the name and that it doesn't recognize it.
